Listen to this article Share …Tinubu’s education reforms yielding results – Alausa Adams Oshiomhole, former Edo State governor, has criticised former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar’s advocacy for the privatisation of tertiary education, arguing that Nigeria cannot afford such a policy while millions of children remain out of school. Oshiomhole spoke on Monday in Abuja at the unveiling of the Renewed Hope Education A+Z Scorecard by Tunji Alausa, Minister of Education. He recalled that Atiku pursued a privatisation agenda while serving as vice-president, questioning the rationale behind his renewed advocacy for private-sector control of tertiary education. Oshiomhole argued that the country should prioritise expanding access to education, particularly for children who are still excluded from the school system, rather than shifting greater responsibility for tertiary education to private operators. The former governor also challenged opposition politicians, particularly Atiku and Peter Obi, former governor of Anambra State, to clarify whether they would retain or abolish the current administration’s education policies if elected into office. He further criticised Atiku over comments he attributed to the former vice-president concerning the use of public resources to enrich friends, arguing that such an approach could undermine funding for education and student support programmes. “If the money he wishes to use to enrich his friends is not diverted to paying student grants, remember that resources are limited at any point in time. That is why economics is about priorities. What is given to those students will not be available to be used to assist friends,” he said. At the event, Alausa also defended the Federal Government’s education reforms against criticism from opposition figures, particularly Obi, accusing him of failing to acknowledge the benefits of the administration’s interventions and misleading Nigerians about some of its policies. The minister cited the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), infrastructure development in tertiary institutions, improved funding and efforts to address staffing shortages as evidence of the government’s interventions in the sector. Responding to Obi’s criticism of the education policies, Alausa said: “What Mr Obi is saying is borne out of ignorance. He needs to read the law. This is the law of Nigeria,” He also accused the former presidential candidate of misleading the public, saying: “If Mr Obi wants to blame me and mislead the public and Nigerians, that tells you the kind of person he is.” On the funding of the student loan scheme, Alausa explained that the four per cent development levy introduced under the Nigeria Tax Act was designed to provide sustainable funding, with 15 per cent of the proceeds allocated to NELFUND. He said the provision was expressly captured in the law and challenged Obi to verify its contents before criticising the government’s funding arrangement. The minister maintained that the administration’s interventions had improved access to tertiary education through student loans and infrastructure upgrades, while the government continued efforts to address shortages of academic staff in universities and other higher institutions.
